words.definition: Abrupt and short in speech or manner, to the point of seeming rude.
words.example: Her brusque 'We're closed' left the tourists standing awkwardly at the door.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'brush' — she brushed me off in one quick, sharp stroke.

words.definition: Noticeably brief in speech, often in a way that feels rude.
words.example: His curt reply, just 'Fine,' told me the conversation was over.
words.mnemonic: 'Curt' looks like 'cut' — he cut his words as short as possible.

words.definition: Using very few words in a smooth but clipped way.
words.example: The general's terse memo contained only three words: 'Hold the line.'
words.mnemonic: 'Terse' rhymes with 'tense' — a tense person spits out short bursts.

words.definition: Rough or abrupt in manner or voice, though often kind underneath.
words.example: The gruff old sailor barked orders but slipped the kids an extra biscuit.
words.mnemonic: 'Gruff' sounds like a dog's low growl — rough, throaty, brusque.

words.definition: Bad-tempered and unfriendly in a sulking, hostile way.
words.example: The surly waiter slammed our plates down and never once smiled.
words.mnemonic: Say it slow: 'sour-ly' — a sour, grumpy attitude toward everyone.

words.definition: Silently gloomy, resentful, and bad-tempered.
words.example: The teenager sat sullen at dinner, arms crossed, refusing to speak.
words.mnemonic: Starts like 'sulk' — picture a kid sulking in silent gloom.

words.definition: Speaking smoothly and easily but without sincerity or real thought.
words.example: His glib apology sounded rehearsed, and no one believed he meant it.
words.mnemonic: 'Glib' sounds like 'glide' — words that glide out too smoothly to trust.

words.definition: Excessively pleased with oneself in a way that irritates others.
words.example: She wore a smug grin after correcting the professor in front of the class.
words.mnemonic: A 'smirk' plastered on a 'mug' (face) = smug.

words.definition: Pretending to be shy or reluctant, often to attract interest.
words.example: When asked if they were dating, she gave a coy smile and changed the subject.
words.mnemonic: 'Coy' rhymes with 'toy' — she toys with you, hiding the real answer.

words.definition: Quiet, gentle, and unwilling to argue or assert oneself.
words.example: The meek intern nodded at every demand, never once pushing back.
words.mnemonic: 'Meek' rhymes with 'weak' — a meek person yields softly.

words.definition: Showing dry, ironic humor, often with a slight twist of the mouth.
words.example: After the plan collapsed, he gave a wry smile and said, 'Went perfectly.'
words.mnemonic: 'Wry' sounds like 'rye' — dry rye humor, twisted like a rye pretzel.

words.definition: Amusing in a quaint, quirky, or unexpected way.
words.example: The professor's droll asides about medieval plumbing kept the lecture lively.
words.mnemonic: 'Droll' sounds like 'troll' doll — an odd little figure that makes you chuckle.

words.definition: Sharp, biting, and bitter in tone, especially when criticizing.
words.example: The critic's acerbic review dismissed the play as 'two hours I want refunded.'
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'acer' (sharp) — hear 'a-sour-bic,' a sour, cutting taste.

words.definition: Bitterly sarcastic and cutting in a way that stings.
words.example: Her caustic remark about his 'genius' plan made the whole room wince.
words.mnemonic: Like a caustic chemical that burns skin — these words burn on contact.

words.definition: Filled with savagely bitter criticism, malice, or hatred.
words.example: The candidate's vitriolic attack on his rival shocked even his own supporters.
words.mnemonic: 'Vitriol' was the old name for sulfuric acid — acid-burning speech.

words.definition: Fiercely critical in a way intended to wound or condemn.
words.example: The critic's scathing review left the young director too embarrassed to attend her own premiere.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'scalding' — a scathing remark burns like scalding water thrown in your face.

words.definition: Sharply perceptive and forceful in expression or argument.
words.example: Her trenchant analysis cut straight to the flaw everyone else in the room had missed.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'trench' — a trenchant point digs a sharp, deep trench right through a weak argument.

words.definition: Bitingly sarcastic, often laced with dark humor.
words.example: His mordant asides at the funeral were so cruel that people laughed before they caught themselves.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'mordere,' to bite — picture a mouth clamping down; mordant wit bites the target.

words.definition: Direct and plainspoken, without softening the truth for politeness.
words.example: 'You're not ready for this job,' she said, blunt as ever, and walked out of the room.
words.mnemonic: A blunt knife has no fine point — blunt speech skips the polite point and just lands flat.

words.definition: Honest and straightforward in manner, holding nothing back.
words.example: When asked about the layoffs, the CEO was refreshingly forthright about exactly how many jobs would go.
words.mnemonic: 'Forth + right' — you go straight forth to the right answer instead of dodging around it.

words.definition: Bold and open in stating opinions, even unpopular or risky ones.
words.example: An outspoken critic of the regime, she was arrested for the columns she refused to soften.
words.mnemonic: 'Out-spoken' — you speak your mind out loud and out into the open, never keeping it in.

words.definition: Showing intense, forceful feeling or conviction.
words.example: His vehement denial, delivered with a pounding fist, only made the jury more suspicious.
words.mnemonic: 'Vee-HE-ment' sounds like a vehicle slamming at a moment's force — feeling that hits that hard.

words.definition: Full of warm, eager passion or devotion.
words.example: An ardent fan, he drove nine hours just to catch ten minutes of the band's soundcheck.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'ardere,' to burn — an ardent heart is one that burns hot with enthusiasm.

words.definition: Filled with intense feeling, especially in a speech or plea.
words.example: Her impassioned plea for mercy moved even the prosecutor to wipe his eyes.
words.mnemonic: 'Im- (into) + passion' — someone has poured pure passion INTO every word they speak.

words.definition: Wildly hurried or agitated by fear, worry, or urgency.
words.example: After losing sight of her son, she made a frantic dash through the crowded mall, calling his name.
words.mnemonic: 'Frenzy' + 'antic' = frantic — the wild, panicky antics of someone in a total frenzy.

words.definition: Impatient and hard to control under restraint or delay.
words.example: The horses grew restive as the storm rolled in, stamping and yanking against their tethers.
words.mnemonic: Looks like 'restless' but resists rest — a restive animal won't stay still and fights the reins.

words.definition: Cautious and watchful of possible danger or trouble.
words.example: Wary of scams, she never once clicked a link in an email she wasn't expecting.
words.mnemonic: 'Wary' hides the word 'war' — in war you stay alert and on guard against every threat.

words.definition: Careful and restrained, unwilling to reveal much.
words.example: He gave the reporter guarded answers, offering nothing that could be traced back to the deal.
words.mnemonic: Picture a sentry standing watch — guarded words sit safely behind a posted guard.

words.definition: Slow to show emotion or share opinions; naturally quiet.
words.example: New colleagues found her reserved for months until, one late evening, she finally opened up.
words.mnemonic: Like a reserved seat held back and kept private — her feelings are held back in reserve.

words.definition: Modest and shy in a quiet, composed way.
words.example: She gave a demure smile and lowered her eyes when the stranger complimented her singing.
words.mnemonic: 'De-mure' sounds like a soft murmur — a demure person speaks and acts in a hushed, modest hush.

words.definition: Shy and easily embarrassed in the presence of other people.
words.example: He gave a bashful wave and stared at his shoes when the girl he liked said hello.
words.mnemonic: One of Snow White's seven dwarfs — Bashful blushes and hides his face the instant anyone looks his way.

words.definition: Lacking in courage or self-confidence and easily frightened.
words.example: Too timid to raise her hand, she let the answer she knew slip away in silence.
words.mnemonic: A 'tiny mouse' is timid — the 'tim-' start sounds like a small, trembling creature that scurries from danger.

words.definition: Nervous and full of fear or apprehension about what might happen.
words.example: The timorous new recruit flinched at every loud noise on the training ground.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'timor' meaning fear (the same root as 'timid') — a timorous person is brimming with 'timor.'

words.definition: Showing embarrassment from an awareness of having done something foolish.
words.example: He offered a sheepish grin after everyone realized he'd been raving about the wrong movie the whole time.
words.mnemonic: Picture a sheep caught chewing your homework — head lowered, giving you that guilty, awkward look.

words.definition: Feeling deep regret and guilt for having done something wrong.
words.example: After breaking the vase, the boy was so contrite that he saved his allowance for a month to replace it.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'con-' (thoroughly) + 'tritus' (ground down) — a contrite heart is worn down and crushed by guilt.

words.definition: Feeling sorrow for one's sins and wishing to make amends.
words.example: Kneeling at the altar, the penitent thief begged the priest to hear his confession.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'penitentiary' and 'penance' — a penitent inmate is doing time and truly feeling sorry.

words.definition: Filled with deep guilt and regret over a past wrong.
words.example: Years later he remained remorseful about the cruel words he'd shouted at his mother.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-morse' = to bite again (Latin 'mordere,' to bite) — the guilt keeps biting you over and over.

words.definition: Showing regret in a wry, resigned, half-amused way.
words.example: She gave a rueful laugh and admitted she really should have listened to the warnings.
words.mnemonic: To 'rue the day' is to bitterly regret it — a rueful smile is the face you make while ruing your choice.

words.definition: Feeling a gentle, sad longing for something lost or out of reach.
words.example: He grew wistful paging through old photographs of the seaside town where he grew up.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'wish-ful' — full of a quiet, aching wish for something you can no longer have.

words.definition: Marked by a deep, thoughtful sadness with no single obvious cause.
words.example: A melancholy mood settled over the empty house once the last of the guests had gone.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'melas' (black) + 'kholē' (bile) — ancient doctors blamed such sadness on an excess of 'black bile.'

words.definition: Appearing lonely, abandoned, and hopelessly sad.
words.example: The forlorn dog sat by the shut gate long after its owner's car had disappeared.
words.mnemonic: From old 'forloren,' meaning utterly lost — hear the '-lorn' as 'lost and alone,' like a puppy left out in the rain.

words.definition: Expressing or filled with sorrow; mournful in look or sound.
words.example: The hound let out a doleful howl every time its master picked up the suitcase.
words.mnemonic: Full of 'dole' — an old English word for grief — so a doleful basset hound's droopy eyes brim with dole.

words.definition: Low in spirits after a disappointment or loss of hope.
words.example: Dejected after the rejection letter, she pushed her dinner around the plate without eating.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'de-' (down) + 'jacere' (to throw) — like 'ejected,' but your spirits are thrown downward.

words.definition: So unhappy that nothing offered can bring any comfort.
words.example: Disconsolate over the loss of her ring, she refused every attempt her friends made to cheer her up.
words.mnemonic: 'Dis-' (not) + 'console' — you simply cannot be consoled; no comfort manages to reach you.

words.definition: Sad and disappointed after a hope or effort has failed.
words.example: The crestfallen team trudged off the field after conceding a goal in the final seconds.
words.mnemonic: Picture a proud rooster whose head-crest has 'fallen' flat after losing the fight — pride and posture collapsed.

words.definition: Dark, gloomy, and grave in mood or appearance.
words.example: The mourners wore black and spoke in hushed, somber tones at the graveside.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'sad' + 'umber' (a dark brown paint) — a dark, sad color.

words.definition: Formal, dignified, and deeply serious in manner or ceremony.
words.example: She made a solemn vow before the judge, her voice steady and grave.
words.mnemonic: SOLE + MN: the 'sole' witness swears an oath with total gravity.

words.definition: Firm, strict, and showing disapproval or harsh discipline.
words.example: The stern headmaster glared until the giggling students fell silent.
words.mnemonic: The 'stern' of a ship is the hard, unyielding back end — like a hard, unyielding face.

words.definition: Extremely harsh, strict, or intense in degree.
words.example: Breaking the treaty brought severe penalties that crippled the nation's economy.
words.mnemonic: SE-VERE sounds like 'so very' — so very harsh.

words.definition: Marked by sharp bitterness and angry, hostile feelings.
words.example: Their acrimonious divorce dragged on for years, each accusation nastier than the last.
words.mnemonic: ACRID + money: an 'acrid' (bitter) fight over money.

words.definition: Unfriendly and openly opposed or aggressive toward someone.
words.example: The crowd turned hostile, jeering and hurling bottles at the referee.
words.mnemonic: Think 'hostage'-takers — unfriendly captors who mean you harm.

words.definition: Actively opposing or showing dislike toward someone or something.
words.example: From the first meeting he was antagonistic, contradicting every point his coworker made.
words.mnemonic: ANTAGONIST — the villain in a story who opposes the hero.

words.definition: Ready and eager to fight or argue.
words.example: The witness grew combative, snapping at the lawyer and refusing to answer calmly.
words.mnemonic: COMBAT + ive: primed for combat.

words.definition: Quick to quarrel or fight; naturally aggressive.
words.example: The pugnacious little terrier snarled and lunged at dogs three times its size.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'pugnus' = fist; also 'pug' the boxer throws punches.

words.definition: Eager for war or aggressive conflict; warlike in attitude.
words.example: The dictator's bellicose speeches promised invasion and rallied troops to the border.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'bellum' = war (as in 'belligerent') — 'belli-' means war.

words.definition: Boldly resisting authority or refusing to obey.
words.example: Arms crossed and chin up, the defiant teenager refused to apologize.
words.mnemonic: DEFY + ant: one who defies.

words.definition: Resisting or rising up against control and authority.
words.example: The rebellious colonists dumped the tea into the harbor to protest the crown.
words.mnemonic: REBEL + lious: a rebel opposes the ruler.

words.definition: Openly rebelling against lawful authority, especially officers or a leader.
words.example: The mutinous sailors seized the captain and locked him below deck.
words.mnemonic: 'Mutiny on the Bounty' — the crew that overthrew its captain.

words.definition: Stubbornly resisting authority, control, or instruction.
words.example: The recalcitrant mule dug in its hooves and would not budge an inch.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'calcitrare' = to kick — 'RE-KICK-itrant', a mule kicking back at every command.

words.definition: Hard to control, manage, or solve; stubbornly difficult.
words.example: Decades of intractable conflict left every peace negotiation in ruins.
words.mnemonic: IN (not) + TRACTable — like a load a tractor can't drag into line.

words.definition: Hard to manage or keep in order; resisting rules and authority.
words.example: The substitute teacher struggled to quiet the unruly class as paper airplanes sailed overhead.
words.mnemonic: Break it up: un + ruly, as in 'rule' — someone who won't be ruled.

words.definition: Turning away from what is expected or proper; willful and hard to guide.
words.example: Their wayward son dropped out of school and vanished for months at a time.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'wants its own way' — always wandering off the right way.

words.definition: Stubbornly refusing to soften a view or feeling despite pleas or reason.
words.example: Despite the family's tears, the judge stayed obdurate and denied the appeal.
words.mnemonic: ob- + Latin durus ('hard') — a heart that has hardened, like 'endure' turned to stone.

words.definition: Refusing to compromise or reach agreement; rigidly holding a position.
words.example: Negotiations collapsed because both sides stayed intransigent, unwilling to give an inch.
words.mnemonic: in- ('not') + transigere ('to come to terms') — literally cannot be brought to terms.

words.definition: Firmly refusing to change your mind despite others' arguments.
words.example: She was adamant that she would pay for the meal herself, waving away every offer.
words.mnemonic: 'Adamant' was the ancient name for the hardest stone (root of 'diamond') — hard as rock.

words.definition: Firmly determined to follow through on a decision or purpose.
words.example: Even after three failed attempts, she remained resolute about reaching the summit.
words.mnemonic: You've made a 'resolution' — you're resolved and won't back down.

words.definition: Firm and unwavering in loyalty, belief, or purpose.
words.example: Through every scandal, his steadfast supporters never once abandoned him.
words.mnemonic: stead + fast = 'stand fast' — planted in place, holding your ground.

words.definition: Very loyal and firmly committed to a person, cause, or belief.
words.example: A staunch defender of free speech, she spoke at every rally in town.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'stanch,' to stop a flow — solid, watertight, unleaking loyalty.

words.definition: Holding on firmly and persistently, refusing to let go or give up.
words.example: The tenacious detective kept working the cold case long after everyone else quit.
words.mnemonic: From Latin tenere ('to hold') — like a 'tenant' gripping the lease and won't move out.

words.definition: Not showing fear or hesitation when facing danger or difficulty.
words.example: She gave an unflinching account of the crash, meeting each juror's eyes.
words.mnemonic: un + flinching — you don't flinch, not even a twitch, when the blow comes.

words.definition: Not discouraged or intimidated by setbacks, danger, or difficulty.
words.example: Undaunted by the storm, the climbers pressed on toward the ridge.
words.mnemonic: un + daunt — nothing 'daunts' (frightens) you; picture courage that can't be dented.

words.definition: Showing great courage and determination, especially in the face of danger.
words.example: The firefighter made a valiant dash into the collapsing house to reach the child.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'valor' and 'value' — full of worth and bravery.

words.definition: Boldly daring, willing to take surprising risks or defy convention.
words.example: The thieves pulled off an audacious daylight heist in front of hundreds of tourists.
words.mnemonic: From Latin audere ('to dare') — say it as 'a-DARE-cious.'

words.definition: Recklessly bold; taking risks without sensible caution.
words.example: It was foolhardy to swim past the buoys with a storm rolling in.
words.mnemonic: fool + hardy — a 'fool' bold ('hardy') enough to do something plainly stupid.

words.definition: A showy display of boldness meant to impress, often masking real fear.
words.example: His swagger was pure bravado; under the table his hands were shaking.
words.mnemonic: 'brave' + a 'show' (-ado) — a performance of courage, not the genuine article.

words.definition: Excessive pride or overconfidence that often blinds a person and invites disaster.
words.example: Blinded by hubris, the general ignored every warning and marched his army into the storm.
words.mnemonic: HUBRIS ≈ 'HUGE-bris': a HUGE ego that swells until it bursts.

words.definition: Behaving as if you are better than others in an unpleasant, overbearing way.
words.example: He was so arrogant that he never bothered to learn a single coworker's name.
words.mnemonic: ARROGANT hides an ARROW — always aiming down at everyone below him.

words.definition: Having far too high an opinion of your own looks, talents, or worth.
words.example: So conceited was she that she checked her reflection in every window she passed.
words.mnemonic: con-SEE-ted: he only ever wants to SEE himself.

words.definition: Treating others as inferior while pretending to be kind or helpful.
words.example: The waiter's condescending tone made the tourists feel like children who couldn't read a menu.
words.mnemonic: CONDESCEND = 'descend' down to someone — talking DOWN from above.

words.definition: Being kind or helpful in a way that reveals a sense of superiority.
words.example: 'Well done, you managed to spell your own name,' she said in a patronizing voice.
words.mnemonic: A PATRON pats you on the head like a lesser being — PAT-ronizing.

words.definition: Acting as though others are beneath you and deserve only disdain.
words.example: The supercilious clerk barely glanced up, as if serving us was beneath him.
words.mnemonic: SUPER + 'cilium' (Latin eyebrow): a raised eyebrow says 'I'm SUPER above you.'

words.definition: Showing that you think someone or something is worthless and beneath respect.
words.example: She gave the cheap imitation a contemptuous glance and set it back down.
words.mnemonic: con-TEMPT: too far beneath you to even TEMPT a second look.

words.definition: Expressing strong dislike and a belief that something deserves no respect.
words.example: The critic was scornful of the film, calling it lazy and beneath discussion.
words.mnemonic: SCORN sounds like SCORCH — a scornful look scorches its target.

words.definition: Expressing mockery and the view that something is ridiculous.
words.example: A derisive snort from the back row told the speaker his idea had flopped.
words.mnemonic: de-RIS (Latin risus, laughter): mocking laughter rising at your expense.

words.definition: To speak about someone or something as unimportant or of little value.
words.example: Rivals tried to disparage her research, dismissing years of careful work as guesswork.
words.mnemonic: 'dis' + PAR: to knock something below PAR, below the standard.

words.definition: To laugh at or make fun of someone in a cruel, mocking way.
words.example: Classmates derided his homemade robot until it actually won the contest.
words.mnemonic: de-RIDE: they take you for a RIDE, mocking you the whole way down.

words.definition: To speak about something in a mocking way that shows you don't believe or respect it.
words.example: Investors scoffed at the tiny startup — until it outsold every competitor.
words.mnemonic: SCOFF is the dismissive snort-cough you give at something you don't buy.

words.definition: To sharply criticize or express strong disapproval of someone's actions.
words.example: The judge rebuked the lawyer for interrupting the witness yet again.
words.mnemonic: RE-BUKE ≈ 'BUCK back': like a horse bucking, you throw the offense back hard.

words.definition: To scold someone with mild, often affectionate disapproval.
words.example: Grandmother chided us gently for tracking mud across her clean kitchen floor.
words.mnemonic: CHIDE rhymes with HIDE — once scolded, the child wants to HIDE.

words.definition: To scold someone loudly and at length in an angry way.
words.example: The coach berated the team for twenty minutes after the sloppy loss.
words.mnemonic: be-RATE: to give someone a brutally low RATING at full volume.
